conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your hospital doctors. I see you came in with very high blood sugar and a fever yesterday. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I felt really bad yesterday. My blood sugar was over 800 when EMS came. I didn’t take my insulin because I got confused about the time. And my foot has been hurting more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also had a fever and some drainage from your left heel ulcer. We’re concerned the infection might be getting into the bone. Did the doctors in the ER start any antibiotics before you left?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They gave me something in the IV and told me to get antibiotics, but I didn’t fill the prescription. I’ve been so overwhelmed with everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ve started you on IV antibiotics here—Vancomycin, Cefepime, and Flagyl—to cover possible bone infection. We also gave you insulin to bring your sugar down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery for my foot? I’m scared of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The vascular surgeon and podiatry team have looked at your case. Because of poor blood flow and the exposed bone, they’re recommending a below-the-knee amputation to stop the infection from spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no… that’s a lot to take in. Can’t we just keep treating it with antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try antibiotics for now, but the infection may not heal without removing the affected area. The team wants to schedule surgery in a few weeks. You’ll go home first to think about it and follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I just want to go home. But I don’t want the infection to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you’re protected. You’ll continue Vancomycin during dialysis and take Cipro and Flagyl by mouth. Blood cultures haven’t grown anything, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my sugar? I usually have help with my meds, but my nurse didn’t come yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your NPH insulin—30 units in the morning—and a sliding scale for corrections. Your sugars are coming down. We’ll keep that plan unless they drop too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My mouth feels dry and I see white patches. Is that from the sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s oral thrush, a yeast infection from high sugar and recent antibiotics. We’ll give you Nystatin swish and swallow to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been constipated. No bowel movement in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’re on Senna and Docusate. We’ll make sure you keep taking those. Staying regular helps with overall comfort and healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs show your hemoglobin dropped a bit, but you’re not losing blood anywhere. It’s likely from your kidney disease. You’ll get your usual Aranesp during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Anemia can cause fatigue, but so can infection and poor sleep. As you heal, your energy should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my heart? I know I’m not on Coumadin anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right. You were off it due to concern for calciphylaxis, but dermatology didn’t see signs of that. Your CHADS2VASc score is high, so your outpatient team should restart anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll talk to them. I don’t want a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had dialysis yesterday and tolerated it well. Your creatinine is coming down—from 3.8 to 2.2—so your kidneys are clearing things better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. How’s my foot looking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ulcer is still there with exposed bone, but no new redness or swelling. The antibiotics are helping control the infection while you decide on surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking… I want to go home. Can I manage the antibiotics there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll get a three-week supply of Cipro and Flagyl, and Vancomycin during dialysis. A nurse will help you at home. Dr. ___’s office will contact you to plan surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain? It’s better with the Dilaudid, but I don’t want to overuse it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send home a small supply for severe pain. Continue Gabapentin and Tylenol for nerve pain. Use the Dilaudid only when needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we did a urine test and found yeast, but you’re not having symptoms, so we won’t treat it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. Antibiotics can disrupt normal balance. We’ll watch it, but no treatment is needed unless you develop symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood work looks stable. White count is down, sugars are controlled, and no fever. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about my bladder? I hate straight cathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We catheterized you this morning. Because you’ve had retention before, we recommend doing it every few days. Call Dr. ___ by tomorrow to discuss how often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call. And I’ll weigh myself daily like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call if you gain more than three pounds. Keep the wound clean, take all meds, and follow up with podiatry and vascular surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m scared about the surgery, but I know it might be necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Take your time. The team will support you every step of the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything. I feel more prepared now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here to help. A nurse will come by with your prescriptions and wound care instructions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get everything arranged. Rest, stay on top of your meds, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Ms. ___. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.
